analyses.title: Evidence Attribution in Visual Document Understanding without Coordinates or Region Labels
analyses.research_question: Can visual document question-answering systems provide reliable, spatially grounded evidence attribution without requiring models to emit coordinates or training data with region-level labels?
analyses.methodology: The paper compares coordinate-based evidence attribution with a language-based interface in which a VLM emits verbatim textual evidence quotes that are subsequently aligned to semantic page regions by a layout parser and multimodal retriever. Six open VLMs are evaluated on a verified 719-question single-document subset of CiteVQA, with answer quality and several evidence-attribution metrics measured under both interfaces. The authors additionally train Qwen3-VL-8B with GRPO using LongDocURL questions and a judge that evaluates answers against gold answers and crops of retrieved evidence regions, without region annotations in the training examples. Error analyses separate failures caused by missing quotations, parser coverage, retrieval assignment, and other attribution errors.

key_findings.finding: Replacing direct bounding-box generation with textual evidence quotations substantially increased evidence recall across all six evaluated open VLMs, from a maximum of 8.1% under coordinate output to 25.9%-46.9% under the language interface.
The language interface sharply reduced attribution hallucination rates, from 82.1%-97.0% with coordinate output to 38.6%-65.4% with language-based attribution.

Answer quality was largely preserved when switching attribution interfaces: five of six backbones changed by no more than 2.3 answer-score points, although Qwen3-VL-8B showed a larger decrease before training.

GRPO training without region labels increased Qwen3-VL-8B evidence recall from 39.9% to 51.3%, reduced attribution hallucination from 41.2% to 28.4%, and raised strict attributed accuracy from 22.4% to 33.8%.

Residual failures under the language interface are dominated by cases in which the model does not quote the necessary evidence at all, while parser misses and quote-to-region assignment conflicts impose additional ceilings.
The method does not eliminate spatial localization from the system; it transfers localization from the VLM output interface to an external layout parser and retriever.

limitations: The experiments are scoped to single-document evidence attribution rather than retrieval and attribution across multiple documents or document versions.
The approach depends on an external layout parser and quote-to-region retriever, so evidence recall cannot exceed the parser's coverage of relevant regions.
The VLM itself does not directly localize evidence geometrically; localization is performed downstream by the parser and retriever.
Evaluation uses a verified subset of 719 questions from 987 single-document CiteVQA validation questions, so results do not cover excluded examples with source or annotation problems.
Figure evidence remains harder to recover than text and tables because textual quotation is a less direct representation of primarily visual evidence.
The paper states that code and configurations will be released, but the examined version does not establish that the promised code release is already publicly available.
raw_claims: Direct coordinate generation performs poorly as an evidence-attribution interface for the evaluated open VLMs.
A model can instead identify evidence with verbatim textual quotations and delegate spatial grounding to a retrieval layer.
Semantic document blocks are produced by a layout parser and matched to model quotations using multimodal retrieval.
The language interface improves evidence recall and precision while substantially reducing hallucinated citations.
Most evaluated backbones retain similar answer quality when coordinates are replaced with textual evidence references.
GRPO can improve attributed answering even when training examples do not contain region-level evidence labels.
The largest remaining error category is failure by the answering model to quote required evidence.
Parser coverage provides an upper bound on what the downstream attribution system can recover.
Tables are handled relatively well by the textual interface, while figure evidence is more difficult.
The study evaluates single-document attribution and does not establish performance for cross-document or cross-version provenance.

analyses.title: VersionRAG: Version-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Evolving Documents
analyses.research_question: Can retrieval-augmented generation explicitly represent document versions and changes so that questions about historical content, version identity, and inter-version differences are answered more accurately and efficiently than version-agnostic RAG?
analyses.methodology: VersionRAG represents evolving documentation as a five-level graph containing category, document, version, content, and change nodes, with temporal links between versions and explicit or automatically derived change information. A query classifier routes content, version, and change questions to specialized retrieval procedures over Neo4j and Milvus Lite, while DeepDiff is used to derive implicit line-level changes when changelogs are unavailable. The authors construct VersionQA with 100 manually curated questions over 34 technical-documentation files and compare VersionRAG against naive vector RAG and Neo4j GraphRAG using Llama 3 8B, GPT-4o Mini, and DeepSeek-R1 70B. GPT-4.1 grades answers against gold references, and the complete set of 100 answers is also manually reviewed.

key_findings.finding: With DeepSeek-R1 70B, VersionRAG achieved 90% overall accuracy on VersionQA, compared with 58% for naive RAG and 64% for the evaluated GraphRAG baseline.

VersionRAG achieved 100% accuracy on the evaluated version-specific content retrieval and version-listing categories with the strongest evaluated model, showing a large advantage on questions that require explicit version identity.

Change-oriented questions remained substantially harder than ordinary content or version questions; the strongest configuration reached 70% change-query accuracy, with implicit changes particularly difficult.

For DeepSeek-R1 70B, VersionRAG used about 186K input tokens and 38K output tokens compared with roughly 2.97M input and 5.92M output tokens for GraphRAG, corresponding to the paper's reported 97% token reduction and substantially lower cost and runtime.
The reported VersionRAG failures were attributed mainly to query misclassification and incomplete change extraction, demonstrating error propagation across the modular pipeline.

The evaluation does not establish that VersionRAG's gains generalize from the small technical-documentation benchmark to domains such as legal, medical, financial, or heterogeneous workplace documents.

limitations: VersionQA contains only 100 questions over 34 technical-documentation files, limiting evidence for cross-domain generalization.
Implicit semantic changes remain difficult: the strongest reported configuration obtains only 60% accuracy on implicit-change questions.
Line-level DeepDiff can miss semantically important changes that are not well represented by textual diffs.

The system assumes that version information can be extracted reliably and that document versions have sufficiently consistent structure; irregular filenames, date-based schemes, or missing metadata can cause failures.
The graph models versions primarily as a sequential history and does not directly represent arbitrary branching, merging, or non-adjacent version dependencies.
Accuracy depends strongly on the underlying LLM; smaller models create fewer useful change nodes and misclassify more queries.
The architecture requires both graph and vector infrastructure and still incurs nontrivial indexing cost.
The pipeline has no end-to-end mechanism that corrects errors introduced by version extraction, change extraction, or query routing.
raw_claims: VersionRAG explicitly stores individual document versions rather than flattening all versions into a common retrieval collection.
Its hierarchy separates documents, versions, version content, and changes between versions.
Queries are classified into content, version, or change-oriented retrieval paths.
VersionQA contains 100 manually curated questions drawn from versioned technical documentation.
Sixty percent of the benchmark questions are version-sensitive.
Naive RAG and the evaluated GraphRAG baseline perform substantially worse than VersionRAG on the complete benchmark with the strongest tested model.
Questions asking about implicit changes are harder than questions supported by explicit changelogs.
The version-aware graph allows retrieved information to retain provenance to a particular version.
VersionRAG requires far fewer indexing-generation tokens than the evaluated GraphRAG pipeline.
Misclassification and incomplete change extraction account for the reported VersionRAG failures.
The authors publicly provide the VersionRAG code and VersionQA dataset.

analyses.title: DocTrace: Towards Traceable Long Document VQA via Hierarchical Evidence Graph Reasoning
analyses.research_question: Can long-document visual question answering be made both more accurate and more traceable by explicitly localizing pages, parsing multimodal page elements, and constructing hierarchical evidence graphs whose nodes provide provenance for the generated answer?
analyses.methodology: DocTrace decomposes long-document VQA into coarse page localization, structured parsing of selected pages into text, table, figure, chart, and other layout elements, and reasoning over an explicit directed evidence graph. Evidence nodes retain semantic content and spatial information, while intermediate reasoning nodes encode dependencies leading to the final answer. Supervision is automatically constructed for answerable and unanswerable cases using Gemini 3.1 Pro as a teacher and GPT-5.5 as a verifier, followed by supervised fine-tuning and task-specific GRPO on Qwen3-VL-8B. The system is evaluated on MMLongBench-Doc, LongDocURL, and SlideVQA with answer metrics, page-localization metrics, graph-validity measures, evidence grounding, ablations, and counterfactual evidence masking.

key_findings.finding: DocTrace improved the Qwen3-VL-8B backbone from 38.5% to 52.9% accuracy on MMLongBench-Doc, from 45.1% to 56.4% on LongDocURL, and from 73.4 to 85.1 F1 on SlideVQA after supervised and reinforcement-learning stages.

Explicit structured parsing and evidence-graph reasoning materially contribute to accuracy: removing structured parsing reduced overall MMLongBench-Doc accuracy from 50.3% to 46.6%, while removing the graph reduced it to 47.2%.
Generated traces showed very high structural validity, including 99.5% evidence grounding, 99.6% graph integrity, and 100% acyclicity and answer connectivity in the reported traceability evaluation.

Counterfactual masking changed answers in 82.8% of cases when cited evidence was masked but only 9.6% when uncited context was masked, indicating that the reported citations are behaviorally associated with answer generation.
The authors explicitly caution that counterfactual masking does not prove that the model's hidden computation internally follows the explicit evidence graph as a causal reasoning program.

Page localization is the major remaining bottleneck, particularly for multi-page questions: Stage-1 evidence coverage is much lower for multi-page than single-page cases, and answer accuracy rises markedly when all gold pages are supplied.

DocTrace reduced reported latency and prefilling load relative to the full-document baseline, with 7.33-second versus 15.04-second latency and 15.5K versus 35.5K prefilling tokens in the reported efficiency comparison.

limitations: The explicit evidence graph provides inspectable provenance but the behavioral tests do not establish that the model's internal computation causally follows that graph.
Stage-1 page localization remains a major bottleneck, especially for questions requiring evidence distributed across several pages.
Hallucination increases when irrelevant distractor pages survive localization, so answer reliability depends strongly on upstream evidence filtering.
Training supervision is automatically generated by a teacher model and validated by another model rather than being entirely human-authored.
The full-parameter training setup uses substantial accelerator resources, which raises the cost of reproducing the training procedure.
The examined paper does not state a public release of the DocTrace implementation or of its complete generated 36,819-instance supervision corpus.
The experiments concern long documents but do not directly model longitudinal document-version identity, cross-version element lineage, or attachment supersession.
raw_claims: DocTrace first localizes a small set of relevant pages in a long visual document.
Selected pages are parsed into layout-aware elements such as text, tables, figures, and charts.
Evidence elements become provenance-bearing nodes in an explicit directed reasoning graph.
The training data distinguish single-page, multi-page, irrelevant-unanswerable, and detail-absent-unanswerable questions.
Supervised fine-tuning is followed by reinforcement learning with rewards for graph faithfulness and answer quality.
DocTrace improves answer scores on all three reported long-document VQA benchmarks relative to its backbone.
Structural parsing and explicit graph construction both contribute independently to performance.
The generated graphs are almost always structurally valid under the paper's graph-validation metrics.
Masking cited evidence affects generated answers far more often than masking uncited context.
The counterfactual experiment demonstrates behavioral dependence but does not prove internal causal execution of the visible graph.
Multi-page performance is strongly constrained by whether the localization stage retrieves every required page.
The generated supervision corpus contains 36,819 instances derived from public benchmarks and additional public documents.

analyses.title: Disambiguating Reference in Visually Grounded Dialogues through Joint Modeling of Textual and Multimodal Semantic Structures
analyses.research_question: Does jointly modeling textual reference relations such as coreference and predicate-argument structure with multimodal mention-to-object grounding improve the resolution of ambiguous and indirect references in visually grounded dialogue?
analyses.methodology: The approach jointly trains textual reference resolution and multimodal reference resolution components that share a text encoder while computing relation-specific similarities between textual mentions and between mentions and detected visual objects. Multimodal grounding uses a frozen Detic detector plus a trainable textual and cross-attention representation, while textual relations include coreference and predicate-argument relations that can supply additional semantic structure for ambiguous mentions. The authors evaluate phrase grounding and multimodal reference resolution on J-CRe3 and Flickr30k-Ent-JP, with additional Japanese textual-reference data used for the textual component. Recall@1, Recall@5, and Recall@10 are reported with an IoU threshold of 0.5, and experiments are repeated with three random seeds.

key_findings.finding: Adding the proposed textual-reference model substantially improved grounding of pronouns in J-CRe3: the coreference-enhanced model achieved Recall@1/5/10 of 0.361/0.683/0.772 versus 0.277/0.527/0.641 for the baseline.

For pronoun grounding, the coreference-enhanced model outperformed both GLIP and MDETR in the reported J-CRe3 comparison, even though GLIP remained stronger on overall phrase grounding at lower recall cutoffs.

Ablation experiments show that introducing textual reference relations improves pronoun grounding, with coreference providing the strongest individual benefit and combining relation types helping noun grounding.

The proposed multimodal-reference model consistently improves Recall@10 over the model without the added textual-reference information and can represent zero-reference cases that the GLIP-plus-parser comparison cannot directly handle.
Textual reference structure increases model confidence for relationships linking mentions, pronouns, predicates, and visually grounded objects in the qualitative analyses.

The results do not establish comparable behavior for non-Japanese dialogue, conversations with more than two participants, or grounding that requires consistent object identity across multiple images or document versions.

limitations: The experiments are limited primarily to Japanese-language data and do not establish multilingual generalization.
The visually grounded dialogue setting contains two-party interactions, so more complex participant structures remain untested.
Some indirect nominative and dative references in J-CRe3 tend to resolve to the master or robot, creating dataset-specific regularities.
The frozen Detic object detector can constrain noun grounding and contributes to weaker noun performance than stronger detection-grounding systems in some comparisons.
Grounding is performed from a single image at a time, making object consistency across changing visual contexts difficult.
The relationship between textual-reference-resolution quality and multimodal-reference-resolution quality requires more repeated and controlled analysis.
The study addresses conversational reference ambiguity but not longitudinal attachment revision, cross-version visual-region identity, or spreadsheet-specific references.
raw_claims: The model treats textual reference resolution and multimodal reference resolution as related tasks rather than independent problems.
The textual and multimodal components share a textual encoder.
Coreference, predicate-argument relations, and other textual links provide signals for disambiguating visually grounded mentions.
J-CRe3 contains visually grounded Japanese dialogue collected from interactions between a human master and an assistive robot.
The proposed textual-reference component provides especially large gains for pronoun grounding.
GLIP remains stronger on some overall phrase-grounding measures even though the proposed method is stronger for pronouns.
Different textual relation types make different contributions to noun and pronoun grounding.
The multimodal model can model references in which a predicate has no corresponding visual object.
Object detection is frozen during the multimodal-reference experiments.
The approach reasons from individual images and does not solve persistent object identity across multiple visual contexts.
The implementation and relevant datasets are publicly linked by the paper.

analyses.title: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Multimomal Generation for Document Question Answering
analyses.research_question: How well do current retrievers, language models, and vision-language models perform on retrieval-augmented document question answering when correct answers require selecting and integrating noisy textual and visual evidence across long multi-page documents?
analyses.methodology: The paper introduces MMDocRAG, a benchmark of 4,055 expert-annotated questions over 222 documents from ten domains, with evidence represented as layout-derived textual or visual quotes and with many questions requiring cross-page or cross-modal evidence. Documents originate from the MMDocIR corpus and are processed with MinerU; visual quotes retain the source image together with OCR text and VLM-generated descriptions. The study evaluates 14 retrieval configurations and 60 language or vision-language models, including several fine-tuned open models, under controlled candidate-evidence sets and end-to-end retrieval conditions. Evaluation covers retrieval recall, text/image quote-selection precision, recall and F1, lexical answer metrics, and LLM-judged fluency, citation quality, text-image coherence, reasoning, and factuality.

key_findings.finding: MMDocRAG contains 4,055 questions, of which 52% require evidence from multiple pages, 39.2% involve multiple images, and 61.7% require cross-modal evidence, making evidence composition a central part of the benchmark.

GPT-4.1 achieved a 70.2 quote-selection F1 and 4.14 answer-quality score with the 20-quote candidate setting, while many open and smaller models showed substantially weaker evidence selection and answer quality.

Performance is lower on interpretative, multi-page, and multi-image questions than on descriptive or single-page questions, showing that evidence composition remains difficult even when candidate evidence is supplied.
Fine-tuning the evaluated open vision-language models on MMDocRAG development data substantially improves their quote selection and answer generation performance.

Using detailed VLM-generated descriptions of visual evidence outperformed relying on OCR text alone in the reported aggregate comparison, indicating that visual semantics not captured by OCR are useful for retrieval and answering.
Text retrievers are stronger for textual evidence, visual retrievers are stronger for image evidence, and hybrid retrieval provides a more balanced solution for mixed-modality questions.
Retrieval errors propagate strongly into generation: GPT-4.1's evidence-selection and answer scores drop markedly when perfect candidate evidence is replaced by actually retrieved evidence.
Evidence appearing later in the supplied candidate context is selected less frequently, revealing a measurable position bias in evidence use.

limitations: The benchmark is built from 222 documents derived from the MMDocIR corpus, so coverage of other document ecosystems, especially evolving workplace attachments, is not established.
The benchmark models page and quote provenance but does not represent longitudinal document versions or lineage between corresponding elements across revisions.
LLM-based answer-quality judging introduces dependence on the selected evaluator and rubric even though complementary automatic metrics are reported.
Controlled candidate-quote experiments measure evidence selection from a supplied pool and are easier than unconstrained retrieval over an entire enterprise document collection.
Comparisons span proprietary and open models with different compute, latency, context, and access characteristics, so aggregate capability differences do not isolate architecture alone.
Direct multimodal processing adds computational and latency overhead, particularly for larger vision-language models.
The observed position bias means evaluation and model behavior can depend on the ordering of otherwise identical evidence.
Retrieval remains a major source of end-to-end degradation even for a strong generator.
raw_claims: MMDocRAG evaluates retrieval and generation jointly for long multimodal documents.
The released benchmark contains 4,055 expert-annotated question-answer pairs over 222 documents.
More than half of the questions require evidence from more than one page.
A majority of the questions require combining information across modalities.
Annotations identify evidence at the quote level in addition to page-level provenance.
Candidate evidence includes both text quotes and image quotes together with deliberately noisy alternatives.
The evaluation separately measures whether a model selects the correct textual and visual evidence.
Large proprietary models lead most reported generation comparisons, but none solves the benchmark completely.
Fine-tuned smaller vision-language models improve substantially relative to their untuned versions.
Detailed visual descriptions provide more useful evidence representations than OCR-only text in the reported comparison.
Text-only and visual retrievers have complementary strengths, motivating hybrid retrieval.
Replacing perfect candidate evidence with retrieved evidence causes a substantial downstream performance loss.
Models are less likely to select relevant evidence when it occurs later in the provided context.
The benchmark and associated code are publicly available through the project's website.
